title: Never break faith
hook: value nothing that makes you break your word or lose self-respect (Meditations 3.7)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was self-control, one of Marcus's four goods. Your line was nothing better.

Curtains can tell you something about a house. Some hang there for warmth, or for sleep. And sometimes a curtain is there for another reason: the purchase nobody mentioned, the deleted message, the plan someone would rather nobody saw. Marcus Aurelius used curtains as a test. In the seventh entry of his third book he lists what a person should never count as worth having, and he ends the list with walls and curtains. Today: never break faith.
screen: `CURTAINS ON A HOUSE.` → `WHAT NEEDS CURTAINS?` → `NEVER BREAK FAITH.`

segments.voice: Never value anything as good for you, Marcus writes, if it will one day force you to break your word or lose your self-respect. Notice the order. He doesn't start with what's forbidden; he starts with what we value. If a thing would cost you your word, it was never really a gain. The list goes on: nothing that makes you hate anyone, suspect anyone, curse anyone, play the hypocrite. Each is a small way of breaking faith, with another person or with yourself. It ends with anything you'd want that needs walls and curtains around it. A plain household test: if a desire only works in hiding, Marcus counts it a loss, however good it looks. It echoes the test from two days ago: think only what you could say out loud. Then he sketches the person who keeps faith. They put their own mind and its goodness first. They don't make a tragedy of things, don't groan, and need neither solitude nor a crowd. They neither chase life nor run from it. Breaking faith is rarely one big betrayal. It's usually small: the call you said you'd make, the favor you said you'd do, the time you said you'd be there. A word that holds in small things is easier to trust in large ones. That's what Marcus is protecting: not a reputation, but a self you can respect.
screen: `NEVER COUNT IT A GAIN IF IT COSTS YOUR WORD.` · `NO HATE, SUSPICION, CURSES, HYPOCRISY.` · `NOTHING THAT NEEDS WALLS AND CURTAINS.` · `THE ONE WHO KEEPS FAITH.` · then, large: `KEEP FAITH.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise that's still open, even a tiny one, like I'll call you back or I'll be there at six, and picture the person who heard you say it. Picture keeping it plainly, without fuss, and rest a moment in what it's like to be someone whose word holds.
Marcus, whose rule was to value nothing that would cost your word, your self-respect, or something that needs walls and curtains. Today's word.
Your line: keep faith. Nothing worth having needs walls and curtains around it. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 543 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HONOR THE POWER OF JUDGMENT.`

what a scholar hears: Marcus's list runs from broken promises to wanting 'walls and curtains', a picture of private vice from a very public man.

chat.says: What does Marcus mean about walls and curtains?
options: If something you want only works in hiding, he counts it a loss, however good it looks.
He means a wise person keeps a private life well hidden from everyone else.

chat.meaning: Marcus says never value anything that needs walls and curtains: a desire that only works in hiding costs your word or self-respect.

Marcus Aurelius.meaning: Roman emperor and Stoic who wrote notes to himself

walls and curtains.meaning: Marcus's image for anything that only works in hiding

breaking faith.meaning: going back on your word, to others or to yourself

notes: 3.7 paraphrased: never value as profitable what compels you to break your promise, lose self-respect, hate, suspect, curse, act the hypocrite, or desire anything needing walls and curtains (Long's wording, from memory). Confirm.
The description of the person who keeps faith (no tragedy-acting, no groaning, needs neither solitude nor many people, neither pursues nor flies from life) is from the remainder of 3.7; confirm.
Greek pistis: confirm that 3.7 uses 'pistin parabenai' (break faith).
